items.evidence: Opened from the weakness review: peers' uncommitted decision rows and queue edits live in the same files, a peer commit swept hunks and a D-number, and landing needs foreign-commit checks before push. Acceptance: one command takes explicit paths and a message, refuses git add -A, takes only this session's hunks from docs/decisions.md and docs/work-queue.json, allocates the next D-number from a lock file so two sessions never share one, refuses to push when git log origin/master..HEAD holds commits not made by this session, and regenerates progress.html and the digests; a two-session fixture on a scratch repo shows no lost row and no duplicate number.

items.title: language: a local may shadow a module-scope function and a builtin type name (reopen D66's reserved set)
items.evidence: Opened from the 2026-11-04 language design review. Problem: E-NAME-0003 ended 35 of the 134 builds that failed on a compile code in 2026-09-20..27, more than any other code (D1678), and its largest slice is the rule that a local or parameter may not reuse a module-scope function (`text`, `row`, `cell`, `level`, `width`, `at`) or a builtin type name (`target`, `Vec`, `i8`). That makes the legality of `let width = 3` depend on declarations elsewhere in the module, which is exactly what a generated line may not depend on (spec section 1, goal 1); D1678's rename fix mitigates it but does not change the design. Proposal: reserve only `use` qualifiers and the `target` namespace. A local or parameter may shadow a module-scope fn, const, var or type name and the builtin type names, because spec section 2 already resolves types and values by position. Module scope keeps one definition per name, so `grep -n ^fn dot` still returns one line, and a call through a shadowed name is a local type error (E-NAME-0004), never an ambiguity. D1678's machine-applicable rename stays for qualifier collisions and duplicate locals. Token and cost: this deletes a repair class. No new syntax, no extra token on any line, a shorter trap section on the card, and it removes one failed build plus one repair turn per occurrence, which is the most expensive failure mode measured. Guard: the five implicit operations, the no-overloading rule and the explicit-cast rule are untouched, and the index, tokens and parse streams keep their shape. Not done: fixtures that shadow a module fn, a const, `i8`, `Vec` and `str` as a value name accept and format; a call through the shadowed name rejects E-NAME-0004; the card re-renders without those two traps; lang-stats repeat rate is re-measured on transcripts written after the change.

items.title: language: cross-module pointer facts come from the declaration, never from the callee's body
items.evidence: Opened from the 2026-11-04 language design review. Problem: the lexical region subset in section 11 plus `callee_keeps` reads another module's body through any number of modules to decide whether a container retains a borrowed pointer. D1677 records the consequence as found and not fixed: a warm build writes an image the clean build refuses with E-SAFETY-0013, and the documented fix adds a body edge per foreign function, so every body edit invalidates its callers and both section 12 and section 15 pay for it. Proposal: a call that hands a region value or a view across a module boundary is legal only against a declared contract on the parameter (`@noescape`, `own`, or `@borrows` for the result direction), which is the fact the interface already serializes in artifact format 14. Nothing outside the function's own lexical scope is read; an unannotated callee gives no answer, so it cannot be inferred from. Token and cost: one attribute line per boundary function that hands region values, in exchange for a warm build that equals a clean one. A silently wrong image costs a rebuild, a bisect and a debugging turn, the most expensive repair class measured, and the checker loses the alias-chain cases that only the body walk accepted, so its own context shrinks. Guard: the single-function rules (move at most once, cleanup on every exit, a view of a mutated container) stay as they are. Not done: D1677's warm and clean builds agree by a fixture; the alias-chain fixtures the walk alone accepted are annotated or moved to @unsafe; both suites pass.

items.title: language: make the zero value total - every enum and union enum declares a member at 0
items.evidence: Opened from the 2026-11-04 language design review. Problem: section 7 carries a carve-out. A type that holds, at any depth, an enum with no member at 0 has no zero value, so `= zero`, a module-scope `var` without an initialiser and `try` in a function returning it are compile errors naming the outermost type and the offending field. A generator must therefore read the whole type graph before it knows whether a line is legal, the same unseen-context dependency as C258. Proposal: an `enum` or `union enum` declaration must name a member whose backing value is 0, the mirror of the existing rule that renames an error whose FNV-1a hash is 0. Then every type has a zero value, and the carve-out, its three error sites and the exceptions in the zero table go. `err` = ok, a slice = nil and the null resource already fit. Token and cost: one member on an enum that starts at 1 (`None = 0`), against a rule and three diagnostics that leave every future context, and generated code writes `= zero` and `try` without first resolving the type. Guard: `= undef` and E-SAFETY-0017, the refusal of a value that can only be invalid, are unchanged. Not done: the section 7 table and rule rewrite, the declaration-time diagnostic naming the enum and the member it needs, accept fixtures for `= zero` and `try` over such an enum, a reject fixture for the declaration without a 0 member, and the card's zero section re-rendered.

items.title: language: protocols are found by an explicit marker, not by a derived snake_case name
items.evidence: Opened from the 2026-11-04 language design review. Problem: `K.hash(v)` resolves to `fn sensor_hash` by deriving the name from the type's name through a Unicode snake_case algorithm (`HTTP2Client` becomes `http2_client`), plus a separate rule for a generic type's stem, a rule for which alias spelling keeps the nominal declaration, and a recorded lookup edge when a supplied fallback is used (section 9, D48). Every implementation must reproduce the algorithm byte for byte, and a reader cannot tell from `fn sensor_hash` that it is the protocol for `Sensor` without running the algorithm in their head. Proposal: `@proto(Sensor)` on the function, and the same fact in `neper index`. Lookup matches a marker rather than a spelling. The five resolution rules, the supplied fallbacks and the call-site syntax stay. Token and cost: one attribute line per protocol function, nothing at any call site, and the spec loses the case algorithm with two name-resolution rules that an agent otherwise has to load to predict a resolution. A typo becomes a missing marker refused with one code, instead of a silent fall back to the supplied hash. Not done: the attribute in the grammar and the checker, the index edge, diagnostics for a duplicated or mismatched marker, and conformance fixtures for a generic type's protocol and the str fallback.

items.title: docs: one normative home per fact (section 13 versus tooling.md, section 11 versus the H-track files)
items.evidence: Opened from the 2026-11-04 language design review. Problem: the same fact is written twice, so a tooling change is read and edited in two places. Section 13 Toolchain is 603 of the spec's 5149 lines and restates docs/tooling.md; section 11's region and concurrency rules restate docs/m25-h02-regions.md and docs/m25-h04-concurrency.md. Three smaller self-contradictions sit on top: `unreachable` is a keyword although section 14 calls it the one builtin that is a keyword rather than a core function; `usize` and `isize` are keywords although they are only type names; section 8 allows copying an `Arena` to transfer it while section 11 makes it affine. Proposal: each fact lives in exactly one document and every other mention links to it. The spec keeps semantics, tooling.md keeps the command and stream contracts, and the H-track files keep their measurements as evidence rather than as normative text. Token and cost: this is the largest context win in the list. An agent landing a tooling change pays for both copies today, and the card, the digest and the tasks page inherit the duplication. Guard: no semantic change; a moved fact gains a link where it was; the card stays generated, never hand-edited. Not done: the split, the three contradictions resolved, and a link check so a moved fact cannot be silently unlinked.

items.title: bootstrap: the card carries the language, not the C bootstrap's defects
items.evidence: Opened from the 2026-11-04 language design review. Problem: docs/llm-neper-card.md tells an author that code under `src/` must also build with the C bootstrap, which refuses `-=` and `x > CONST {` and truncates a function past 256 locals silently. Those are bootstrap defects printed as language rules. A generator avoids legal syntax and still cannot know when the truncation bites, and a clean bootstrap build is not proof of anything. Proposal: the card carries the language and nothing else. The bootstrap either accepts the surface the grammar defines or it is gone, which is C088, the first queue row. Until then the card carries one sentence pointing at C088 instead of a list of shapes to avoid. Token and cost: the card is loaded on nearly every edit turn, so a `src/`-only exception list is tokens spent on a defect the self-host build would catch anyway, and a silently truncated function costs a debugging session. Not done: the card source edit and re-render, and either the three bootstrap fixes with a fixture per shape or C088's closure.

items.title: language: labelled break and continue
items.evidence: Opened from the 2026-11-04 language design review; this is the one addition the review recommends. Problem: v1 has no labels, so a generated loop that must leave two levels writes a flag local, an `if` guard at every level and a check after the inner loop. That is three lines and a mutable binding per nesting level, all of which a reviewer follows to see where control goes. Proposal: an optional label on `for` and `while` with `break outer` and `continue outer` resolved at parse time, no dynamic behaviour, no new keyword. Token and cost: measured rather than assumed. Add the shapes to benchmarks/tokens/profile.py and to the card's token table before the grammar revision; the labelled form must be no worse than the flag form per nesting level, which it should beat by roughly ten tokens at depth two, and the tokens and parse streams gain a label field. Guard: `break` and `continue` without a label mean what they mean today, and a label that names no enclosing loop is a compile error. Not done: the grammar revision, the parser, the checker, the formatter and the card re-render; two fixture programs at depth two and three, checked against the flag spelling; the token profile updated.

items.title: a syntax error exits with its diagnostic: the error path must not consume the machine
items.evidence: Found while porting x.duckdb.duckdb to DuckDB v2 and trying to build the Linux self-hosted compiler: a parse failure in lib/e/str.e (mem.bitcast[f32], syntax the September bootstrap does not know) did not report and exit. Measured in a freshly restarted 5GB WSL instance with nothing else running, RSS went 3148 kB at t=3s to 4352956 kB at t=6s, then 4550256 kB at t=9s, with MemAvailable down to 15MB, the process in D state, and exit code 1 only after the allocator had exhausted the VM. The diagnostic printed correctly (E-SYNTAX-9999 at four sites); the defect is that emitting it retained 4.5GB and stalled on swap for minutes instead of returning. Acceptance: a program with a syntax error reports every diagnostic it currently reports and exits 1 with peak RSS within a small fixed multiple of the source size (measured, and stated in the fixture); the same failure on Windows and Linux; a fixture that parses a file with many errors and asserts the exit code and a bounded peak; and no error path allocates per-diagnostic state that is never released.

items.title: the bootstrap builds the tree again: refresh it, or make the seed path the contract
items.evidence: Found while getting tests/selfhost to reach its DuckDB fixture. build/windows/neper.exe and build/linux/neper are both 0.0.96-neper0 and neither can parse the current tree: lib/e/str.e:13 stops at a function type as a struct member, src/check.e:924 at a type-member limit. The bootstrap is a fixed point -- it must parse what it builds -- so once the language gains syntax it cannot build src/main.e, and the suite fails at selfhost.ps1:39 'self-hosted compiler slice did not build'. Windows only appeared healthy because a self-hosted compiler from 6 Nov sat in build/; Linux had nothing until run.sh gained the NEPER_SEED path run.ps1 already had (83bc973bb), and a compiler cross-emitted from the Windows self-host works as that seed. Acceptance: a bootstrap that builds the current src/main.e on both hosts with no NEPER_SEED set, and a suite run on a clean checkout that reaches its fixtures; or, if the seed becomes the contract, both runners require NEPER_SEED and fail with one message naming how to produce it; plus a check that asserts the bootstrap parses the tree so this cannot rot silently again.

items.title: emitted binaries are reproducible: no field may depend on which compiler binary ran
items.evidence: Found while verifying 18 bootstrap-lint fixes by differential build. Two compilers built from the same command line, from source states that differ only by the fix, emit binaries that differ in exactly 8 bytes on many fixtures and match on others. The 8 bytes sit inside an ASCII field `!003d88c0<8 hex>:...` in the image, and the control proves they track the compiler binary rather than the code: the untouched Nov 6 self-hosted compiler differs from a current build in the same 8 bytes at the same offset on the same fixture. Emitting the same source twice with the SAME compiler is byte-identical, so this is not general nondeterminism. The consequence is that byte-identical output cannot be used to check a codegen change, which is the cheapest and strongest regression test available: masking the field is required before any build comparison, and that masking is knowledge held outside the tree. Acceptance: identify what the 8 hex digits hash (candidate: the compiler image, its build id, or a toolchain signature), make the field a function of the translation unit and not of the compiler that performed it, or document it as an intentional stamp in the binary format's spec; a check that builds one source with two different compiler binaries and compares the images byte for byte, so this cannot regress silently; and the header comment in the emitted image's format doc stating whether reproducibility across compiler builds is promised.

items.title: the artifact path emits the same debug info as the whole-program path
items.evidence: Found once crew_windows could finally be reached: 'crew_windows at -j 1 is not the image linked from its artifacts (--time)'. Repro: emit-em-all over crew_windows then link-em the twelve artifacts, and separately emit-executable the same fixture at -j 1, both in the default (debug) mode. Sizes 75560 linked against 76072 direct. A PE section compare (dumpbin /headers) shows every section identical except .debug_info: 3FFA virtual / 4000 raw linked, against 4068 / 4200 direct -- the whole 512-byte file difference is that section's rounding. The code is byte-identical: 0 differing bytes across 0x400..0xB000, which is the headers' payload, .text (A8F5/AA00) and .idata (1B0/200). Inside .debug_info the first four bytes are the unit length, 0x3FF6 linked against 0x4064 direct, and the streams diverge at +0x10A6: the linked copy lists `e.os.PollRegistration`, the direct one `e.text.utf8.Iterator`, so the subprogram DIEs are in a different order and 110 bytes differ in total. In --release the two paths are byte-identical (E5321649... both), which is why this has never been seen: release emits no debug info to disagree about. Pre-existing and not this session's: the untouched Nov 6 self-hosted compiler produces the same two hashes (C1E733B0... linked, FE538AEC... direct). Acceptance: the artifact path and the whole-program path emit the same .debug_info for the same program in the default mode, so the two images are byte-identical there as they already are in --release; crew_windows' artifact comparison then covers both modes again; and a check pins the two images byte for byte in a debug build, which is what would have caught this before a suite run had to reach line 1067 to notice. Where the order comes from, located for the fix: the PE path assembles the debug rows in `assemble_vars` (src/em_link.e:558, D1582: 'The named locals of every copied function, placed where its code landed, in code order: what the image's DWARF describes'), reached from `link_artifact_image` (src/main.e:7744). Code order is already the stated intent, so the artifact path is ordering its subprogram DIEs by the function table it builds from artifacts rather than by where the code landed, while the whole-program path emits them in source order. So the fix is to sort both by code offset, not to reorder the CU. Deferred rather than attempted here: it is an emitter change on a path that only a debug build exercises, the code itself is already byte-identical, and crew_windows now asserts byte-identity in --release where it holds.

items.evidence: Partial. Baseline now 82.8% (4,172 runs): main.e 69.2%, tool.e 88.2%; still unreached in main.e: hot-load paths, wasm and device commands, compare-manifests. Still unreached in main.e: apply-plan, compare-manifests, fmt-project, test-impact-file, emit-shared-library, wasm run, hot-load paths and the CLI error paths. Entry points found and added to scripts/coverage-run.sh on a 5-run sample: emit-object x64/aarch64 linux (object_elf 79%), aarch64 none/neperos (link_image_a64 78%), wasm32 --threads --source-map (wasm_threads 100%, wasm_map 97%), dis-file --json (disasm_x64 45%). glsl.e stays 0%: every gpu_* fixture aborts valgrind with an aspacem out_of_memory on all targets, so it needs the D776 instrumented route. Still open: tool.e, emit_a64, main.e, platform, binary, msl, emit_x64 and the test/run/eval/index/fmt commands. Original baseline (2026-11-11, 3,702 runs, 65.5%) glsl.e, disasm_x64.e, object_elf.e, wasm_map.e and link_image_a64.e are 0%, wasm_threads.e 10%, tool.e 12.9%, emit_a64.e 25%, main.e 32%, platform.e 33%, binary.e 48%, msl.e 54%, emit_x64.e 56%. The --gpu glsl fixtures sampled never reached glsl.e, so find the entry point for each (a command, a flag, a target such as aarch64 none or neperos) and add a fixture or conformance case that fails if it breaks. items.title: compiler coverage reaches 100% with a ratchet floor in the suite
items.evidence: Open, after C304. Baseline 2026-11-11 (C303, docs/coverage-floor.txt = 65.0): check.e 87.2% (13,248/15,197), lower.e 91.5%, codegen_x64.e 91.1%, em.e 67.2%, parse.e 75%, lex.e 69.6%, resolve.e 71.3%, nir.e 75.8%, graph.e 82.7%. Close gaps by phase (front end, check, lower/nir/graph/regalloc, em and codegen and linkers), one negative and one positive fixture per diagnostic code from the error table, golden-byte checks for emit_*.e encoders, @test unit tests where fixtures are awkward (first verify src modules are importable from a test). Then the suite fails when coverage drops below the committed floor, the floor rising per merged item until it is 100% with only docs/coverage-exempt.tsv entries uncovered. Keep run.sh and run.ps1 in parity. Wire the floor as: tests/selfhost/run.sh and run.ps1 run coverage_report.py --floor $(cat docs/coverage-floor.txt); add docs/coverage-exempt.tsv (file, line, reason); keep scripts/check_suite_parity.py green.
